content: Prolonged labour can result in significant risks for both the mother and the baby. For the mother, these risks include exhaustion, postpartum haemorrhage, and sepsis. For the baby, complications such as fetal distress and asphyxia may occur. These risks are particularly pronounced in settings with limited medical resources. Early detection and appropriate clinical interventions are essential to mitigate these risks. Active management of labour, as opposed to a physiological or expectant approach, has been shown to reduce the likelihood of prolonged labour. The use of antispasmodic medications during labour has been proposed as a strategy to facilitate faster and more effective cervical dilatation. These medications may serve as either a preventative or therapeutic measure to reduce the incidence of prolonged labour. However, the evidence supporting their efficacy remains largely anecdotal, necessitating a systematic review of the available data to provide a more definitive answer. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of antispasmodic medications on labour in term pregnancies. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, ProQuest, the University of Stellenbosch dissertation database, and Google Scholar, as of February 28, 2013. Reference lists of relevant articles were also reviewed, and pharmaceutical companies and field experts were contacted. No language restrictions were applied. The review included randomised controlled trials that compared the use of antispasmodics with either a placebo or no medication in women with term pregnancies. Two independent reviewers screened abstracts, selected studies for inclusion, assessed the risk of bias, and extracted data. Any missing data were addressed by contacting the authors of the trials. A total of 21 trials, involving 3286 participants, were included in the review. Of these, 17 trials (2617 participants) were included in the meta-analysis. The antispasmodics evaluated included valethamate bromide, hyoscine butyl-bromide, drotaverine hydrochloride, rociverine, and camylofin dihydrochloride. Most studies incorporated antispasmodics as part of an active labour management protocol. The overall quality of the studies was poor, with only four trials assessed as having a low risk of bias. Thirteen trials (1995 participants) reported on the duration of the first stage of labour. The administration of antispasmodics significantly reduced the duration of the first stage by an average of 74.34 minutes (mean difference [MD] -74.34 minutes; 95% confidence interval [CI] -98.76 to -49.93). Seven studies (797 participants) reported on the total duration of labour, which was reduced by an average of 85.51 minutes (MD -85.51 minutes; 95% CI -121.81 to -49.20). Six studies (820 participants) provided data on the rate of cervical dilatation, which was significantly increased by an average of 0.61 cm/hour (MD 0.61 cm/hour; 95% CI 0.34 to 0.88). The use of antispasmodics did not affect the duration of the second and third stages of labour. Additionally, the rate of normal vertex deliveries was not influenced by the administration of these medications. Only one study examined pain relief following the use of antispasmodics, but no definitive conclusions could be drawn from this data. There was significant heterogeneity in most outcomes, prompting the use of random-effects meta-analysis. Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore the sources of heterogeneity, but these analyses did not provide clear explanations. Maternal and neonatal adverse events were inconsistently reported. The primary maternal adverse event noted was tachycardia, while no serious neonatal adverse events were reported. In conclusion, the evidence suggests that antispasmodics may reduce the duration of the first stage of labour and increase the rate of cervical dilatation, but the quality of this evidence is low. There is very low-quality evidence to support a reduction in the total duration of labour. Moderate-quality evidence indicates that antispasmodics do not affect the rate of normal vertex deliveries. There is insufficient evidence to draw conclusions about the safety of these medications for mothers and babies. Large, well-designed randomised controlled trials are needed to further evaluate the effects of antispasmodics on prolonged labour, particularly in the context of expectant labour management.
